stimulus.title: Plasmolysis in onion cells
stimulus.text: Students peeled thin layers of epidermis from two groups of red onions: onions grown with normal watering and onions grown under drought. They placed pieces in sucrose solutions for 20 minutes and, under a microscope, counted 100 cells per piece, recording how many were plasmolyzed. Each value is the mean of four pieces.

table.caption: Percent of onion epidermis cells plasmolyzed after 20 minutes in sucrose

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between sucrose concentration and the percent of plasmolyzed cells in the normally watered onions.

rubric.point: States that the percent of plasmolyzed cells increases as sucrose concentration increases (with few or none plasmolyzed below 0.2 mol/L and nearly all by 0.6 to 0.8 mol/L).
accept: as sucrose concentration increases, more cells are plasmolyzed
positive relationship between sucrose concentration and percent plasmolyzed
plasmolysis rises from about 0% at 0.2 mol/L to 100% at 0.8 mol/L

parts.sample: As sucrose concentration increases, the percent of plasmolyzed cells increases: almost none are plasmolyzed at 0.2 mol/L or below, about half at 0.4 mol/L, and all of them at 0.8 mol/L.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the data, calculate the difference, in percentage points, between the two groups at 0.4 mol/L sucrose, and identify the sucrose concentration at which about half of the drought-grown cells are plasmolyzed.

rubric.point: Difference of 35 percentage points (51 − 16) AND about 0.5 mol/L for the drought-grown half point.

parts.sample: At 0.4 mol/L, 51% − 16% = 35 percentage points more of the normally watered cells were plasmolyzed. About half of the drought-grown cells (48%) were plasmolyzed at 0.5 mol/L.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of water potential, why cells become plasmolyzed in the stronger sucrose solutions.

rubric.point: In strong sucrose the solution has a lower water potential than the cell, so water leaves the cell (from higher to lower water potential) and the cytoplasm and membrane shrink away from the cell wall.
accept: the solution is hypertonic, with lower water potential, so water moves out of the cell by osmosis and the membrane pulls away from the wall
water leaves the cell toward the more negative water potential outside, so the protoplast shrinks from the wall

parts.sample: More sucrose makes the solution's water potential lower (more negative) than the water potential inside the cell. Water moves by osmosis from higher to lower water potential, so it leaves the cell. The cell wall is rigid, so as the contents lose water the membrane pulls away from the wall: plasmolysis.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A student claims that drought-grown onion cells contain a higher concentration of dissolved solutes than normally watered cells. Justify the claim using the data, and explain how this difference could help a plant growing in dry soil.

rubric.point: Uses the data (drought-grown cells need a stronger sucrose solution, about 0.1 mol/L more, before the same share plasmolyzes, or fewer are plasmolyzed at each concentration from 0.2 to 0.6 mol/L) AND explains that more solute gives a lower water potential inside the cells, so water can still move from dry soil into the root cells.
accept: half point shifts from about 0.4 to 0.5 mol/L, so their cells hold more solute and have lower water potential, which keeps water flowing in from drier soil
fewer drought cells plasmolyze at every middle concentration; more solute lowers the cells' water potential below the soil's so they still take up water

parts.sample: Drought-grown cells needed a stronger solution to plasmolyze: half were plasmolyzed at about 0.5 mol/L compared with about 0.4 mol/L for normally watered cells, and at 0.4 mol/L only 16% were plasmolyzed against 51%. A solution must have a lower water potential than the cell to draw water out, so the drought-grown cells have a lower water potential, which means more dissolved solute. In dry soil, the soil water's water potential is low; cells with more solute keep their water potential below the soil's, so water still moves into the roots.
